claim: From observations in rodents, it has been suggested that the cellular basis of learning-dependent changes detected using structural MRI may be increased dendritic spine density.
source: From observations in rodents, it has been suggested that the cellular basis of learning-dependent changes, detected using structural MRI, may be increased dendritic spine density, alterations in astrocyte volume, and adaptations within intracortical myelin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Keifer et al., 2015) as indicated in the full manuscript text.

claim: From observations in rodents, it has been suggested that the cellular basis of learning-dependent changes detected using structural MRI may be alterations in astrocyte volume.
source: From observations in rodents, it has been suggested that the cellular basis of learning-dependent changes, detected using structural MRI, may be increased dendritic spine density, alterations in astrocyte volume, and adaptations within intracortical myelin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kleim et al., 2007; Woo et al., 2018) as indicated in the full manuscript text.

claim: From observations in rodents, it has been suggested that the cellular basis of learning-dependent changes detected using structural MRI may be adaptations within intracortical myelin.
source: From observations in rodents, it has been suggested that the cellular basis of learning-dependent changes, detected using structural MRI, may be increased dendritic spine density, alterations in astrocyte volume, and adaptations within intracortical myelin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (McKenzie et al., 2014; Keiner et al., 2017; Kougioumtzidou et al., 2017; Zatorre et al., 2012) as indicated in the full manuscript text.

claim: Myelin plasticity is crucial for neurological function.
source: Myelin plasticity is crucial for neurological function, and active myelination is required for learning and memory.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Active myelination is required for learning and memory.
source: Myelin plasticity is crucial for neurological function, and active myelination is required for learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the Introduction section (McKenzie et al., 2014; Geraghty et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2020; Steadman et al., 2020).

claim: The dynamics of myelin plasticity and how it relates to morphometric-based measurements of structural plasticity remains unknown.
source: However, the dynamics of myelin plasticity and how it relates to morphometric-based measurements of structural plasticity remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Whole-brain VBM revealed nonlinear decreases in gray matter volume juxtaposed to nonlinear increases in white matter volume within GM that were best modeled by an asymptotic time course.
source: Whole-brain VBM revealed nonlinear decreases in gray matter volume (GMV) juxtaposed to nonlinear increases in white matter volume (WMV) within GM that were best modeled by an asymptotic time course.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from VBM analysis presented in the study.

claim: Using an atlas-based cortical mask, nonlinear changes with learning were found in primary and secondary motor areas and in somatosensory cortex.
source: Using an atlas-based cortical mask, we found nonlinear changes with learning in primary and secondary motor areas and in somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from masked VBM analysis.

claim: Analysis of cross-sectional myelin immunoreactivity in forelimb somatosensory cortex confirmed an increase in myelin immunoreactivity followed by a return towards baseline levels.
source: Analysis of cross-sectional myelin immunoreactivity in forelimb somatosensory cortex confirmed an increase in myelin immunoreactivity followed by a return towards baseline levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data presented in the study.

claim: Quantitative confocal microscopy confirmed changes specifically to the length density of myelinated axons.
source: Further investigations using quantitative confocal microscopy confirmed these changes specifically to the length density of myelinated axons.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in the study.

claim: The absence of significant histological changes in cortical thickness suggests that nonlinear morphometric changes are likely due to changes in intracortical myelin.
source: The absence of significant histological changes in cortical thickness suggests that nonlinear morphometric changes are likely due to changes in intracortical myelin for which morphometric WMV in somatosensory cortex significantly correlated with myelin immunoreactivity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the absence of cortical thickness changes combined with observed myelin changes.

claim: Morphometric WMV in somatosensory cortex significantly correlated with myelin immunoreactivity.
source: The absence of significant histological changes in cortical thickness suggests that nonlinear morphometric changes are likely due to changes in intracortical myelin for which morphometric WMV in somatosensory cortex significantly correlated with myelin immunoreactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between MRI and histological data.

claim: These observations indicate a nonlinear increase of intracortical myelin during learning.
source: Together, these observations indicate a nonlinear increase of intracortical myelin during learning and support the hypothesis that myelin is a component of structural changes observed by VBM during learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in the study.

claim: Myelin is a component of structural changes observed by VBM during learning.
source: Together, these observations indicate a nonlinear increase of intracortical myelin during learning and support the hypothesis that myelin is a component of structural changes observed by VBM during learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the correlation between VBM and histological findings.

claim: Longitudinal structural MRI of the human brain has revealed experience-dependent local changes in estimates of gray matter volume.
source: Longitudinal structural MRI (sMRI) of the human brain has revealed experience-dependent local changes in estimates of gray matter volume (GMV) (Draganski et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Draganski et al., 2004).

claim: Recent evidence suggests that changes in GMV follow a nonlinear pattern throughout training.
source: Recent evidence suggests that these changes in GMV follow a nonlinear pattern throughout training (Wenger et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Wenger et al., 2017b).

claim: Macroscopic plasticity of brain structure determined by sMRI has been directly associated with neuronal dendritic spine plasticity together with astrocyte reorganization in the absence of cell proliferation.
source: Macroscopic plasticity of brain structure determined by sMRI has been directly associated with neuronal dendritic spine plasticity together with astrocyte reorganization in the absence of cell proliferation (Keifer et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2021), in which these plastic changes were observed to be transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Keifer et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2021).

claim: Plastic changes in dendritic spines and astrocytes were observed to be transient.
source: Macroscopic plasticity of brain structure determined by sMRI has been directly associated with neuronal dendritic spine plasticity together with astrocyte reorganization in the absence of cell proliferation (Keifer et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2021), in which these plastic changes were observed to be transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Observations using two-session sMRI indicated macrostructural volumetric increases within areas involved in motor control, sensory processing, learning, and memory.
source: Furthermore, observations using two-session sMRI (before vs. after training) indicated macrostructural volumetric increases within areas involved in motor control, sensory processing, learning, and memory (Badea et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Badea et al., 2019).

claim: Using ex vivo diffusion tensor imaging, significant white matter differences have been observed in WM underlying motor cortex.
source: At the microstructural level, using ex vivo diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), significant white matter (WM) differences have been observed in WM underlying motor cortex (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2013), as well as experience-dependent DTI differences observed in GM structure (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2013).

claim: Experience-dependent DTI differences have been observed in GM structure.
source: At the microstructural level, using ex vivo diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), significant white matter (WM) differences have been observed in WM underlying motor cortex (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2013), as well as experience-dependent DTI differences observed in GM structure (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2020).

claim: Increases in intracortical myelin may reduce estimates of GMV.
source: However, changes in intracortical myelin may also affect estimates of GMV, such that increases in intracortical myelin may reduce estimates of GMV, and the inverse, for which decreases in intracortical myelin may increase estimates of GMV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical properties of myelin and MRI signal characteristics.

claim: Decreases in intracortical myelin may increase estimates of GMV.
source: However, changes in intracortical myelin may also affect estimates of GMV, such that increases in intracortical myelin may reduce estimates of GMV, and the inverse, for which decreases in intracortical myelin may increase estimates of GMV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical properties of myelin and MRI signal characteristics.

claim: Myelin plasticity driven by both neuronal activity and experience has been described.
source: Myelin plasticity is critical for learning and memory, and myelin plasticity driven by both neuronal activity and experience has been described (Gibson et al., 2014; Mensch et al., 2015; Swire and Ffrench-Constant, 2018; Bacmeister et al., 2020; Wake et al., 2011; Makinodan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Active myelination by newly recruited oligodendrocytes has been shown to be necessary for learning and memory.
source: Active myelination by newly recruited oligodendrocytes has been shown to be necessary for learning and memory (McKenzie et al., 2014; Geraghty et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2020; Steadman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The learning of a novel skilled reaching task in rodents is associated with functional reorganization of cortical motor maps, including an expanded representation of the trained limb.
source: In addition, the learning of a novel skilled reaching task in rodents is associated with functional reorganization of cortical motor maps, including an expanded representation of the trained limb (Kleim et al., 1998; Kleim et al., 2004; Tennant et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Functional remapping during motor learning is accompanied by synaptogenesis, increased spine formation, and glial changes.
source: This functional remapping is accompanied by a variety of structural and functional changes, including synaptogenesis, increased spine formation, and glial changes (Kleim et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Learning in a forelimb skilled-reaching paradigm transiently suppresses oligodendrogenesis while increasing oligodendrocyte precursor cell differentiation, oligodendrocyte maturation, and myelin sheath remodeling in forelimb motor cortex.
source: It was very recently described that learning in a forelimb skilled-reaching paradigm transiently suppresses oligodendrogenesis while increasing oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) differentiation, oligodendrocyte maturation, and myelin sheath remodeling in forelimb motor cortex (Bacmeister et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Bacmeister et al., 2020).

claim: Learning-induced suppression of oligodendrocytes was transient but left OPC differentiation unaffected.
source: Learning-induced suppression of oligodendrocytes was transient but left OPC differentiation unaffected, which suggests that learning may temporarily decrease survival and integration of differentiated OPCs as mature myelinating oligodendrocytes (Bacmeister et al., 2020), in line with previous work in the developing central nervous system (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Bacmeister et al., 2020).

claim: Learning may temporarily decrease survival and integration of differentiated OPCs as mature myelinating oligodendrocytes.
source: Learning-induced suppression of oligodendrocytes was transient but left OPC differentiation unaffected, which suggests that learning may temporarily decrease survival and integration of differentiated OPCs as mature myelinating oligodendrocytes (Bacmeister et al., 2020), in line with previous work in the developing central nervous system (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on inference from cited research.

claim: Successful reaches and accuracy during motor skill training significantly increased with time in trained mice.
source: Successful reaches and accuracy during motor skill training significantly increased with time (F11,364 = 25.50, p<0.001 and F11,364 = 7.976, p<0.001, respectively) in trained mice (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The improvement in accuracy was confirmed by an improvement in successful reaches on first attempt throughout the learning paradigm.
source: The improvement in accuracy was confirmed by an improvement in successful reaches on first attempt throughout the learning paradigm (F11, 364 = 10.56, p<0.001; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At experimental day 14, trained animals successfully retrieved 47 ± 3% pellets with accuracy of 18 ± 3%.
source: At experimental day 14, trained animals successfully retrieved 47 ± 3% pellets with accuracy of 18 ± 3% while nontrained control mice performed significantly lower (t = 8.641, df = 45, p<0.001) than trained mice with only 7 ± 2% successful reaches and an average accuracy of 10 ± 2%.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral performance data.

claim: Nontrained control mice performed significantly lower than trained mice with only 7 ± 2% successful reaches and an average accuracy of 10 ± 2%.
source: At experimental day 14, trained animals successfully retrieved 47 ± 3% pellets with accuracy of 18 ± 3% while nontrained control mice performed significantly lower (t = 8.641, df = 45, p<0.001) than trained mice with only 7 ± 2% successful reaches and an average accuracy of 10 ± 2%.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral performance data and statistical comparison.

claim: VBM analyses revealed changes in GMV and WMV in trained and in nontrained control mice.
source: VBM analyses revealed changes in GMV and WMV in trained and in nontrained control mice (SI Appendix, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by VBM analysis results shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Three different regression models revealed statistically significant changes in both GMV and WMV.
source: Three different regression models – linear, asymptotic, and quadratic (SI Appendix, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), representing three different time courses – were used and revealed statistically significant changes in both GMV and WMV (pFDR corr<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical modeling of MRI data.

claim: Significant nonlinear decreases in GMV relative to the control group were observed juxtaposed with significant nonlinear increases in WMV during learning.
source: Significant nonlinear decreases in GMV relative to the control group were observed juxtaposed with significant nonlinear increases in WMV during learning (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by VBM analysis results shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The asymptotic model provided a much higher number of significant voxels than either the linear or quadratic models.
source: Interestingly, the asymptotic model provided a much higher number of significant voxels than either the linear or quadratic models and there were no significant linear changes in WM associated with learning (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model results shown in Table 1.

claim: There were no significant linear changes in WM associated with learning.
source: Interestingly, the asymptotic model provided a much higher number of significant voxels than either the linear or quadratic models and there were no significant linear changes in WM associated with learning (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results shown in Table 1.

claim: Significant decreases in GMV and significant increases in WMV were observed in both cortical and subcortical brain areas.
source: Significant decreases in GMV and significant increases in WMV were observed in both cortical and subcortical brain areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by VBM analysis results.

claim: Asymptotic modeling revealed GMV decreases in discrete brain areas including primary motor cortex, primary somatosensory cortex for the forelimb, and globus pallidus.
source: Clusters for which AIC values indicated asymptotic modeling revealed GMV decreases in discrete brain areas including primary motor cortex (MOp), primary somatosensory cortex for the forelimb (SSp-ul), and globus pallidus (GPe) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by AIC-based model selection and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Quadratic modeling revealed GMV decreases in the paramedian lobule and vermian lobule VI of cerebellum, superior colliculus, and nucleus accumbens.
source: whereas clusters for which AIC values indicated preferred quadratic modeling revealed GMV decreases in the paramedian lobule (PRM) and vermian lobule VI of cerebellum (DEC), superior colliculus (SC), and nucleus accumbens (ACb; Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by AIC-based model selection and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Asymptotic modeling demonstrated statistically significant decreases in GMV that overlapped with significant increases in WMV in cortical sensorimotor areas in trained animals relative to nontrained controls.
source: This analysis demonstrated that asymptotic modeling was clearly preferred and that statistically significant decreases in GMV (pFDR corr<0.001) overlapped with significant increases in WMV (pFDR corr<0.01) in cortical sensorimotor areas in trained animals relative to nontrained controls (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by masked VBM analysis results shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Changes were observed in primary motor areas and somatosensory cortex for forelimb and hindlimb contralateral to the trained limb.
source: These were observed in primary motor areas (MOp) and somatosensory cortex for forelimb and hindlimb (SSp-ul and SSp-ll) contralateral to the trained limb, somatosensory barrel field (SSp-bf) ipsilateral to the trained limb, and bilateral secondary motor areas (MOs) and bilateral somatosensory area for the mouth (SSp-m).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical localization of VBM results.

claim: Nonlinear decreases in GMV and increases in WMV relative to nontrained controls were observed contralateral to the trained limb in sensorimotor cortex based on fMRI mapping.
source: Nonlinear decreases in GMV and increases in WMV relative to nontrained controls were observed contralateral to the trained limb.
evidence: This claim is supported by VOI analysis based on independent fMRI data.

claim: These changes followed a nonlinear model rather than a linear one.
source: These changes followed a nonlinear model rather than a linear one (Δ AICc > 2; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by AIC-based model comparison shown in Table 3.

claim: The nonlinear decreases in GMV together with nonlinear increases in WMV observed during motor learning in somatosensory cortex span from layer IV through layer VIa.
source: The nonlinear decreases in GMV together with nonlinear increases in WMV observed during motor learning in somatosensory cortex span from layer IV through layer VIa (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical localization using the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A significant correlation was observed between WMV extracted using an unbiased fMRI-based VOI and myelin immunoreactivity in trained animals.
source: We observed a significant correlation between WMV, extracted using an unbiased fMRI-based VOI from an independent study (Jung et al., 2019), with myelin immunoreactivity in trained animals (Figure 5B; Pearson's r = 0.75, p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between MRI and histological data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A nonsignificant negative trend was found between GMV and myelin immunoreactivity.
source: In line with this result, we found a nonsignificant negative trend between GMV and myelin immunoreactivity (Figure 5B; Pearson's r = –0.38, p=0.35).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The quantification of myelin immunoreactivity within the bilateral cluster located in SSp-ul revealed significant changes with training.
source: The quantification of myelin immunoreactivity within the bilateral cluster located in SSp-ul revealed significant changes with training (one-way ANOVA, F5,66 = 2.538, p<0.05; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Myelin immunoreactivity increased up until experimental day 6 after which it began to decrease toward baseline levels.
source: Specifically, myelin immunoreactivity increased up until experimental day 6 after which it began to decrease toward baseline levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunohistochemical data over time.

claim: From baseline measurements, average MBP immunoreactivity increased by 15% at experimental day 6 followed by an 8% decrease from experimental day 6 to experimental day 14.
source: From baseline measurements, at experimental day 0, average MBP immunoreactivity increased by 15% at experimental day 6 followed by an 8% decrease from experimental day 6 to experimental day 14.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunohistochemical data.

claim: The differences detected in myelin immunoreactivity preferentially followed a nonlinear model rather than linear.
source: In line with our observations using VBM, the differences detected in myelin immunoreactivity preferentially followed a nonlinear model rather than linear (Δ AICc > 2) with an 87.8% probability of a preferred nonlinear model compared to a linear model.
evidence: This claim is supported by AIC-based model comparison of immunohistochemical data.

claim: No significant differences were observed in myelin immunoreactivity between trained animals and nontrained controls at experimental day 14.
source: No significant differences were observed in myelin immunoreactivity between trained animals and nontrained controls at experimental day 14 (t = 0.4096, df = 22, p>0.05) (SI Appendix, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of immunohistochemical data.

claim: No significant difference was observed in cortical thickness between trained mice and nontrained controls.
source: No significant difference was observed in cortical thickness between trained mice and nontrained controls (t = 0.5561, df = 98, p>0.05, n animals = 72 for trained mice, n animals = 28 for nontrained controls).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cortical thickness measurements.

claim: No difference was found in the cumulative distribution of cortical thickness between groups.
source: Similarly, no difference was found in the cumulative distribution of cortical thickness between groups (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p>0.05, D = 0.08949, n = 424 for trained mice, n = 191 for nontrained controls).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cortical thickness distribution.

claim: A correlation was found between learning rate and WMV, where animals with WMV that best fit an asymptotic model exhibited higher learning rates.
source: We evaluated WMV data extracted from the fMRI VOI contralateral to the trained limb at experimental day 14 and found a correlation between learning rate and WMV (Figure 5G) (Pearson's r = –0.378, p=0.0360). Animals in which changes in WMV presented a larger similarity to an asymptotic time course (lower AICc values) exhibited a higher learning rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral and MRI data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There is a significant increase in the length density of myelinated axons from baseline to experimental day 6 followed by a significant decrease toward baseline levels at experimental day 14.
source: There is a significant increase in the length density of myelinated axons from baseline to experimental day 6 followed by a significant decrease toward baseline levels at experimental day 14 (one-way ANOVA, F2,7 = 8.249, p<0.05; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The length density of myelinated axons increased 175% from baseline to experimental day 6 and decreased 60% from experimental 6 to experimental day 14.
source: Specifically, the length density of myelinated axons increased 175% from baseline to experimental day 6 and decreased 60% from experimental 6 to experimental day 14.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of confocal microscopy data.

claim: The length density of myelinated axons follows a nonlinear quadratic model.
source: Furthermore, the length density of myelinated axons follows a nonlinear quadratic model (F2,7 = 8.249, p<0.05; Figure 6B) with an R2 of 0.7021.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical modeling of confocal microscopy data.

claim: The changes detected in length density of myelinated axons follow a quadratic model rather than a linear one with a 99.35% probability.
source: The changes detected in length density of myelinated axons follow a quadratic model rather than a linear one (AIC > 2) with a 99.35% probability of a preferred quadratic model compared to a linear model.
evidence: This claim is supported by AIC-based model comparison.

claim: Length density is influenced by the remodeling of existing myelin sheaths and the addition of new myelin onto previously unmyelinated regions of axons.
source: Length density is influenced by the remodeling of existing myelin sheaths and the addition of new myelin onto previously unmyelinated regions of axons, either by newly recruited or preexisting oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological mechanisms that could explain the observed changes in length density.

claim: Nonlinear morphometric changes are likely due to changes in intracortical myelin rather than changes in cortical thickness or surface area.
source: This multimodal approach indicates that nonlinear changes observed in cortical GMV and WMV using VBM are likely caused by changes in tissue composition (e.g., more intracortical myelin, as suggested by the immunodetection analyses) rather than changes in cortical thickness or surface areas of SSp-ul, which are unlikely to happen in the relatively short period of a 15-day learning paradigm.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combination of MRI and histological findings.

claim: WMV calculated from WM-segmented T1-weighted MRI using an MT pulse represents myelin to a substantial degree.
source: Therefore, WMV calculated from WM-segmented T1-weighted MRI using an MT pulse represents myelin to a substantial degree.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between WMV and myelin immunoreactivity.

claim: The nonlinear increase of intracortical myelin observed at experimental day 6 is produced by increased, or de novo, myelination of axons in cortical circuits rather than increases in the diameter of the existing myelinated axons.
source: Taking into consideration the observations from confocal microscopy of myelinated axons, we speculate that the nonlinear increase of intracortical myelin observed at experimental day 6 is produced by increased, or de novo, myelination of axons in cortical circuits rather than increases in the diameter of the existing myelinated axons.
evidence: This is speculation based on the confocal microscopy findings.

claim: Oligodendrocyte development has been reported to be required for motor learning in adult mice within the first hours after being introduced to the complex wheel running learning paradigm.
source: Consistent with this idea, oligodendrocyte development has been reported to be required for motor learning in adult mice within the first hours after being introduced to the complex wheel running learning paradigm (Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: The nonlinear changes observed in somatosensory cortex for the forelimb match with the well-characterized reorganization of forelimb representation during motor skill learning using electrophysiological measurements.
source: As well, the nonlinear changes observed in somatosensory cortex for the forelimb match with the well-characterized reorganization of forelimb representation during motor skill learning using electrophysiological measurements (Tennant et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior electrophysiological research.

claim: Changes in ipsilateral motor cortices are consistent with fMRI findings in humans showing bilateral MOp activation during the execution of a unilateral high-precision motor task.
source: Changes in ipsilateral motor cortices are consistent with fMRI findings in humans showing bilateral MOp activation during the execution of a unilateral high-precision motor task (Buetefisch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior human fMRI research.

claim: Bilateral activation was attributed to an inhibitory effect from ipsilateral motor cortex on contralateral motor cortex.
source: This bilateral activation was later attributed to an inhibitory effect from ipsilateral motor cortex on contralateral motor cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation from prior research.

claim: This inhibitory effect was modulated by the demand on accuracy of the motor task.
source: Interestingly, this inhibitory effect was modulated by the demand on accuracy of the motor task (Wischnewski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Wischnewski et al., 2016).

claim: Ipsilateral changes in GMV and WMV with learning may be attributed to existing interhemispheric circuits that are strengthened or modified through adaptive myelination.
source: Thus, ipsilateral changes in GMV and WMV with learning may be attributed to existing interhemispheric circuits that are strengthened or modified through adaptive myelination.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed bilateral changes and prior research on interhemispheric circuits.

claim: The study of experience-dependent volumetric changes in primary motor cortex in human adults trained to write and trace with their nondominant hand revealed a bilateral GMV expansion followed by a partial renormalization.
source: In contrast with our findings of GMV decreases, the study of experience-dependent volumetric changes in primary motor cortex in human adults, trained to write and trace with their nondominant hand, revealed a bilateral GMV expansion followed by a partial renormalization (Wenger et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior human research (Wenger et al., 2017b).

claim: The WMV enlargement observed in GM by VBM and by myelin immunohistochemistry exhibits an initial expansion, followed by a (partial) renormalization.
source: The WMV enlargement we observed in GM by VBM and by myelin immunohistochemistry exhibits an initial expansion, followed by a (partial) renormalization.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed temporal pattern in the data.

claim: These observations support the hypothesis that myelin is, at least in part, a component of an expansion-renormalization model comprising exploration, selection, and refinement stages.
source: These observations support the hypothesis that myelin is, at least in part, a component of an expansion-renormalization model comprising exploration, selection, and refinement stages (Wenger et al., 2017a; Makino et al., 2016; Lindenberger and Lövdén, 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the data and theoretical framework from cited research.

claim: Newly formed connections are likely strengthened in response to repetitive firing of neural circuits produced by a discrete sequence of movements.
source: It is likely that newly formed connections are strengthened in response to repetitive firing of neural circuits produced by a discrete sequence of movements (Milner et al., 1998).
evidence: This is speculation based on established principles of neural plasticity and cited research.

claim: The increased activity within these circuits likely stimulates additional myelination of involved axons to provide increased efficiency.
source: The increased activity within these circuits likely stimulates additional myelination of involved axons to provide increased efficiency.
evidence: This is speculation based on the relationship between neural activity and myelination.

claim: Experiments utilizing two-photon imaging after inducing monocular deprivation revealed neuron-class-specific myelin plasticity.
source: Experiments utilizing two-photon imaging after inducing monocular deprivation revealed neuron-class-specific myelin plasticity, suggesting that reconfiguration of network connectivity after sensory deprivation requires precise tuning of individual myelination profiles instead of a broad addition of myelin (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Yang et al., 2020).

claim: Reconfiguration of network connectivity after sensory deprivation requires precise tuning of individual myelination profiles instead of a broad addition of myelin.
source: Experiments utilizing two-photon imaging after inducing monocular deprivation revealed neuron-class-specific myelin plasticity, suggesting that reconfiguration of network connectivity after sensory deprivation requires precise tuning of individual myelination profiles instead of a broad addition of myelin (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a suggestion from cited research (Yang et al., 2020).

claim: Once the optimal circuitry is selected and refined, active myelination is no longer required to support recall and execution of a pre-learned skill.
source: Interestingly, once the optimal circuitry is selected and refined, active myelination is no longer required to support recall and execution of a pre-learned skill (McKenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (McKenzie et al., 2014).

claim: The majority of structural changes with learning follow a nonlinear pattern, suggesting that expansion followed by (partial) renormalization is a rather general phenomenon across regions.
source: Our whole-brain analysis comparing the different possible time-course models identified that the majority of structural changes with learning follow a nonlinear pattern, suggesting that expansion followed by (partial) renormalization is a rather general phenomenon across regions and may be a common principle that unites many manifestations of structural plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the whole-brain VBM analysis results.

claim: There is a large, yet nonsignificant increase in myelin immunoreactivity during the pre-training days, suggesting that pre-training and task familiarization is sufficient to trigger formation of new neuronal connections, stimulating myelination.
source: Moreover, there is an interestingly large, yet nonsignificant increase in myelin immunoreactivity during the pre-training days, suggesting that pre-training and task familiarization is sufficient to trigger formation of new neuronal connections, stimulating myelination.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed trends in the data.

claim: A previous study in mice showed that the proliferation of OPCs was accelerated in motor cortex within just 4 hr of exposure to the complex wheel.
source: Consistent with this idea, a previous study in mice showed that the proliferation of OPCs was accelerated in motor cortex within just 4 hr of exposure to the complex wheel.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The introduction to a novel skill learning paradigm stimulated OPC differentiation into newly forming oligodendrocytes after just 2.5 hr of self-training.
source: In addition, the introduction to a novel skill learning paradigm stimulated OPC differentiation into newly forming oligodendrocytes after just 2.5 hr of self-training (Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: Myelination is a rapid and dynamic plastic change throughout learning.
source: Although previous results using the SRT (Bacmeister et al., 2020) suggested that production of myelin does not appear until days or weeks later (for review, see Bonetto et al., 2021), here we observe that myelination is a rapid and dynamic plastic change throughout learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed rapid changes in myelin immunoreactivity in this study, contrasting with prior research.

claim: Higher learning rates were associated with a nonlinear/asymptotic model of the changes in the MRI-derived WMV.
source: Higher learning rates were associated with a nonlinear/asymptotic model of the changes in the MRI-derived WMV.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between learning rate and model fit.

claim: The selection and refinement phases of the expansion-renormalization model highly influence the proficiency of learning at the individual level.
source: We could speculate that the selection and refinement phases of the expansion-renormalization model highly influence the proficiency of learning at the individual level.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed relationship between learning rate and WMV changes.

claim: Learning-induced reinforcement of selected circuits by myelination may contribute to improved communication and oscillatory synchrony within or between distributed neural populations.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that the learning-induced reinforcement of selected circuits by myelination contributes to improved communication and oscillatory synchrony within or between distributed neural populations (Noori et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation based on cited research about the role of myelination in neural communication.

claim: This plasticity may serve to stabilize oscillatory neural activity across brain regions to facilitate and preserve learned behaviors.
source: This plasticity may serve to stabilize oscillatory neural activity across brain regions to facilitate and preserve learned behaviors.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the observed plasticity.

claim: The quadratic changes in myelin immunoreactivity observed by densitometry appear to be influenced by an increase in the length density of myelinated axons followed by a decrease toward baseline levels.
source: The quadratic changes in myelin immunoreactivity observed by densitometry appear to be influenced by an increase in the length density of myelinated axons followed by a decrease toward baseline levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between densitometry and confocal microscopy findings.

claim: The observed increase in length density during the acquisition phase of learning goes in accordance with the idea of an exploration phase of learning associated with the production of substantial number of novel candidate circuits.
source: The observed increase in length density during the acquisition phase of learning goes in accordance with the idea of an exploration phase of learning associated with the production of substantial number of novel candidate circuits (myelinated axons).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of the expansion-renormalization model.

claim: During the consolidation phase of learning, optimal candidate circuits to carry out the task will be selected and refined, for which increases in myelin sheath diameter may occur.
source: Afterward, during the consolidation phase of learning, optimal candidate circuits to carry out the task will be selected and refined, for which increases in myelin sheath diameter may occur.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms underlying the consolidation phase.

claim: A strong correlation between T1-weighted signal intensity and mGM was reported while no correlation was found between signal intensity and cortical thickness.
source: A strong correlation between T1-weighted signal intensity and mGM was reported while no correlation was found between signal intensity and cortical thickness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Chung et al., 2017).

claim: Since no significant changes in cortical thickness were found during learning and it is unlikely that changes in surface area were produced during the 15-day learning paradigm, the morphometric changes observed during learning are consequence of changes in GM and WM density and not volume.
source: Since we did not find significant changes in cortical thickness during learning and that it is unlikely that changes in surface area were produced during the 15-day learning paradigm, we can assume that the morphometric changes observed during learning are consequence of changes in GM and WM density and not volume.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of cortical thickness changes and the short duration of the study.

claim: This assumption is in line with the changes observed in myelin immunoreactivity at the histological level.
source: Furthermore, this assumption is in line with the changes we observed in myelin immunoreactivity at the histological level.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the MRI and histological findings.

claim: Motor learning dynamically modulates macrostructural brain plasticity.
source: In this study, we found that motor learning dynamically modulates macrostructural brain plasticity, identified nonlinear decreases in GMV juxtaposed to nonlinear increases in WMV, and that these changes are associated with adaptive myelination in forelimb sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's main findings.

claim: These changes are associated with adaptive myelination in forelimb sensorimotor cortex.
source: In this study, we found that motor learning dynamically modulates macrostructural brain plasticity, identified nonlinear decreases in GMV juxtaposed to nonlinear increases in WMV, and that these changes are associated with adaptive myelination in forelimb sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's main findings.

claim: A total of 123 young-adult (8- to 11-week-old) male C57BL/6J mice were used in the study.
source: A total of 123 young-adult (8- to 11-week-old) male C57BL/6J mice (Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME) were used in the study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Mice were food-restricted 1 week prior to behavioral training to reach 85–90% of their free-feeding weight.
source: Mice were food-restricted 1 week prior to behavioral training. Food restriction was performed gradually to reach 85–90% of their free-feeding weight (calculated by a nonfood-restricted control group).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: T1-weighted images were acquired using an MT pulse for increased contrast between tissue types with different transfer susceptibilities.
source: T1-weighted images were acquired using an MT pulse for increased contrast between tissue types with different transfer susceptibilities.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition method.

claim: A T1 3D FLASH sequence was used with MT-weighting by Gaussian-shaped off-resonance irradiation performed at 9.4 T with 100 μm isotropic spatial resolution.
source: We used a T1 3D FLASH sequence (TR/TE = 50/8 ms, flip angle = 20°, using four repetitions) with MT-weighting by Gaussian-shaped off-resonance irradiation (30 μT MT pulse, frequency offset 1.5 kHz, pulse duration 1.8 ms, flip angle 351.2°) performed at 9.4 T (Bruker BioSpec 94/20, running Paravision 6.0 software) with 100 μm isotropic spatial resolution using a 1H Quadrature transmit/receive MRI cryogenic mouse brain RF coil (MRI CryoProbe, Bruker, Germany) for signal reception.
evidence: This is a detailed description of the MRI acquisition parameters.
